Two wrong options are not equivalent merely because both are wrong. Respect distinctions the task actually tests, including syntax, units and boundaries; do not invent an unstated preference or restriction to obtain one answer.

Before accepting, try to make every non-key alternative satisfy the literal stem under a valid interpretation. Test the actual wording, not just the familiar pattern you expect. A standard or sufficient construction is not automatically the only valid construction. Look for a permitted counterexample to any claim of necessity, including must, only, always or cannot. Require any minimum, placement, preference, representation or domain restriction in the stem or supplied rules; never supply it merely to exclude an alternative. If another offered answer works or a material ambiguity remains, reject the unchanged item.

Check the supplied explanations themselves, including their calculations, comparisons and claims about what a distractor means or how it was obtained. A correct key does not excuse false feedback. Reject a demonstrated defect; use uncertain if you cannot establish whether the complete response is sound. Judge each response independently, even when others look similar.

Return only the required audits object. For each supplied ID, give reason first: a brief, concrete finding or supporting check, at most 600 characters. Ground the finding in the supplied content and justified facts; do not speculate about unseen learner actions or how the content was produced. Then give verdict: accepted, rejected or uncertain. Your reason may name counterexamples or corrected calculations to explain a finding, but do not rewrite or return a replacement question, key, or feedback. The application can release only the exact original content of an accepted response.
